hero.prompt: A friendly flat cartoon of a Kenyan home kitchen: a charcoal jiko with a sufuria on top, a wooden mwiko, a chopping board with sliced onions, an open wooden door, and a shelf holding a closed recipe book with a pot picture on its cover.
hero.alt: A drawing of a Kenyan kitchen with a jiko, a sufuria, a mwiko, a chopping board with onions and a recipe book on a shelf.

slides.title: Predict: What do all cells share?
slides.subtitle: Think alone first. Write three sentences.
slides.time_note: Silent writing, as in the SoW (3 minutes).

blocks.text: A girl smiling and holding up one finger with a neat plaster on it, beside a chopping board with sliced onions.
items: amina_healing_finger

A friendly flat cartoon of one teenage girl in a school uniform smiling and holding up one hand with a neat plaster on her finger, standing beside a kitchen table with a wooden chopping board of sliced onions.

blocks.text: Platelets, neutrophils, fibroblasts and skin cells helped heal Amina's finger. They look different. What do ALL cells share?
Write 3 sentences in your notebook.
items: I think all cells share… because…

do: Before learners enter, display the phenomenon image: Amina's healing finger (the cross-section diagram from Lesson 1).
Show this slide. Learners work alone in their science notebooks.
Start the 3:00 timer.
Walk around quietly and scan notebooks. Do not collect them.
say: Before we learn anything new today, I want you to predict.
Look at Amina's finger. All those different cells working together. What do you think every single one of them has in common?
Write three sentences. Start with: I think all cells share… because…
notes.wait_time: The full 3 minutes of silence. Do not speak.
look_for: Scan 8 to 10 notebooks: each learner has written at least 3 sentences before pair share starts.
Listen and look for: a membrane, genetic material, a control centre, a nucleus.
Note any learner who writes 'I don't know'. Give them support during Observe.
if_then: If a learner writes 'I don't know', say: Think of two cells from Amina's finger. What parts might both have? Write one guess and one reason.
If a learner writes 'all cells have a nucleus', do not correct. Say: Interesting. Let's hold that idea and test it today.
notes.why_this_works: Writing a prediction alone brings out what learners already think before any teaching. This shows the teacher the misconceptions (for example, 'all cells have a nucleus') that the lesson will test.
answer_key: Any honest prediction with a reason is accepted. Example: I think all cells share a cell membrane, because every cell needs a boundary. I think all cells share DNA, because they all came from the same body. I think they may all have a nucleus, because the nucleus controls the cell.

slides.title: Pair share
slides.subtitle: Talk with your shoulder partner.
slides.time_note: Pair share is 90 seconds in the SoW; the rest of the slide time is for moving to the sharing slide.

items: speech :: Read your 3 sentences to your partner.
ear :: Listen to your partner's ideas.
handshake :: Agree on one idea to share.

do: Learners turn to a shoulder partner.
Start the 1:30 timer.
Walk around and listen. Choose 3 pairs to call on next.
say: Turn to your shoulder partner. Read your sentences to each other.
Listen carefully. Then agree on one idea you can share with the class.
look_for: Both partners speak. Note pairs that mention a membrane, genetic material or a nucleus.
if_then: If a pair is silent, say: Start with your 'because'. Why did you think that?
notes.why_this_works: Saying an idea aloud to one partner is a low-risk step before speaking to the whole class. More learners are ready to share.

slides.title: BEFORE — Our Predictions
slides.subtitle: Ideas from the class. We do not correct them yet.
slides.time_note: SoW shares 3 pairs and records key words. Kept short to fit the period.

blocks.text: Key words from your ideas go on the board.
items: We will test these ideas today.

do: Write OUR PREDICTIONS as a column heading on the board. Write BEFORE — Our Predictions beside it.
Cold-call 3 pairs: one pair that mentioned a membrane or genetic material, one pair that wrote 'nucleus', and one pair you did not hear from yet.
Write the key words on the board.
Ask for a hands-up count: Who wrote that every cell has a nucleus? Write the number on the board. You will return to it in Explain.
say: Pair at the window table, what did you agree on?
Thank you. Interesting. Let's hold that idea and test it today.
notes.wait_time: 5 seconds after each name before they answer.
look_for: Pairs give a reason, not only an idea.
if_then: If a pair gives a wrong idea, do not correct. Say: Interesting. Let's hold that idea and test it today.
notes.why_this_works: Writing predictions where everyone can see them makes learners want to check them later. Not correcting keeps learners willing to share.

slides.title: The ugali kitchen
slides.subtitle: Same basic tools. Set up in different ways.
slides.time_note: SoW Part A is 15 minutes in all (trimmed to 12). This is part 1 of 2.

blocks.text: A drawing of a Kenyan kitchen with a jiko, a sufuria, a mwiko, a chopping board with onions and a recipe book on a shelf.
items: ugali_kitchen

A friendly flat cartoon of a Kenyan home kitchen: a charcoal jiko with a sufuria on top, a wooden mwiko, a chopping board with sliced onions, an open wooden door, and a shelf holding a closed recipe book with a pot picture on its cover.

blocks.text: Which part of the kitchen is like the cell membrane, the part that controls what comes in and out?

do: Draw a simple kitchen outline on the board. Label it: door = cell membrane; recipe book on shelf = nucleus/DNA; jiko (stove) = mitochondria; sufuria, mwiko, chopping board = organelles.
Tell the analogy story, then pause.
Ask the question on the slide. Cold-call 2 learners.
say: Every kitchen in Nairobi, whether in a Kibera home or a Westlands restaurant, has these basics.
But the kitchen in a hospital canteen is set up differently from a home kitchen in Kericho. Same tools, different arrangement, different job.
That is exactly what we will discover about cells.
What part of the kitchen would you say is like the cell membrane, the thing that controls what comes in and out?
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds of silence after the story. 12 seconds after the question.
look_for: Learners link 'controls what comes in and out' to the door. Note who can explain why.
if_then: If no one answers, say: Think about who or what can pass through the door of a kitchen. Who decides?
notes.why_this_works: A familiar kitchen gives new cell words something to attach to, so there is less to remember. Learners reuse the same picture all lesson. Misconception addressed: a cell is not just a blob; it is organised.
notes.science_note: Use this one mapping all lesson. Limits of the analogy: a kitchen door is opened and shut by a person. A cell membrane controls what passes without anyone deciding. A jiko makes heat by burning fuel. Mitochondria release energy from food inside the cell.

slides.title: Map the kitchen to the cell
slides.subtitle: Work in groups of four. Fill in your notebook table.
slides.time_note: SoW Part A is 15 minutes in all (trimmed to 12). This is part 2 of 2.

do: Groups of four discuss, then each learner copies and completes the two-column table in their notebook.
Circulate. Check two tables per group.
say: Talk in your group. Which cell part is each kitchen feature like?
Fill in the table in your own notebook.
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds after each prompt before you help.
look_for: Check two tables in each group: at least 5 correct mappings.
Listen for reasons such as 'the door controls what goes in and out'.
if_then: If a group maps the jiko to the membrane, say: The jiko makes heat from fuel. Which cell part releases energy from food?
If a group has fewer than 5 rows filled, say: Look at the kitchen picture. What does each thing do? Which cell part does a similar job?
notes.why_this_works: Matching a known kitchen to unknown cell parts links new words to things learners already understand. Doing it in a group lets learners argue about their choices.
answer_key: Door = cell membrane.
Recipe book on the shelf = nucleus (DNA).
Jiko (stove) = mitochondria.
Sufuria = an organelle (a cell part with a job).
Mwiko and chopping board = organelles.

slides.title: Study: an animal cell
slides.subtitle: Read the labels. What jobs might these parts do?
slides.time_note: SoW Part B is 20 minutes in all (trimmed to 15). Split over four slides.

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.

do: Show the diagram. If printed A3 sheets or ARES cards are available, learners may use them as well.
Give learners 1 minute of silent looking. Then ask them to point to the parts and name them in pairs.
say: This is a generalised animal cell. Look at the labels.
Which parts did you put in your kitchen table?
look_for: Learners name parts without reading the label.
if_then: If learners are not sure of a part, say: Read the label. Then tell your partner what it might do.
notes.why_this_works: Studying the diagram first gives every learner the same evidence to use in the card sort.

slides.title: Study: a plant cell
slides.subtitle: What is the same as the animal cell? What is different?
slides.time_note: Part 2 of 4 for SoW Part B.

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.

do: Show the diagram.
Ask pairs to find 2 parts that are in the animal cell and 2 parts that are only in this cell.
say: Compare this with the animal cell. What do you see here that was not in the animal cell?
look_for: Learners find the cell wall and the vacuole as extra parts.
if_then: If a learner cannot find a difference, say: Look at the outside of the cell. What is there?
notes.why_this_works: Comparing two diagrams helps learners spot patterns themselves before the teacher names them.

slides.title: Study: a prokaryotic cell
slides.subtitle: This is a bacterium such as E. coli.
slides.time_note: Part 3 of 4 for SoW Part B.

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.

do: Show the diagram.
Ask pairs: Which parts do you see here that were in the other two cells? Which are missing?
Do not play any ARES video now. Videos on this topic can give away the card sort answers.
say: This is a prokaryotic cell, a bacterium such as E. coli.
Look at it next to the animal and plant cells. What is the same? What is missing?
look_for: Learners notice that the DNA is not inside a nucleus.
if_then: If learners do not see the difference, say: Where is the DNA in the animal cell? Where is it here?
notes.why_this_works: Seeing the three cells one after another gives learners the evidence they need for the card sort.

slides.title: Cell theory: three scientists
slides.subtitle: Read. Then fill in the table.
slides.time_note: Part 4 of 4 for SoW Part B.

rows: How it connects to Amina's healing

blocks.text: Write one sentence for each scientist about Amina's finger.

do: Learners read about the three scientists on their ARES resource cards or printed sheets, then fill in the table.
Circulate. Check that every row has a sentence in the last column.
say: You will read about three scientists. Each added one piece to the cell theory puzzle.
As you read, fill in your Evidence Table. For each scientist, write one sentence that connects their idea to Amina's healing finger.
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds after each prompt before you help.
look_for: Check 8 to 10 notebooks: every scientist row has a completed last-column sentence. A blank row means the learner cannot yet connect theory to observation.
if_then: If a learner is stuck on Virchow, say: Virchow said all cells come from pre-existing cells. How does that explain where the new skin cells on Amina's finger came from?
notes.why_this_works: Linking each scientist to Amina's finger stops learners from just copying names and dates. History becomes evidence for the phenomenon. Misconception addressed: new cells appear from nothing.
answer_key: Schleiden | Germany, 1838 | A botanist. He said all plants are made of cells. | Amina was cutting onions. Onions, like her finger, are made of cells.
Schwann | Germany, 1839 | He studied animal cells. He said animals are made of cells too. | Amina's skin, blood and muscle cells are all cells.
Virchow | Germany, 1855 | All cells come from pre-existing cells (omnis cellula e cellula). | New skin cells on Amina's finger came from skin cells that were already there.

slides.title: Sort: prokaryote or eukaryote?
slides.subtitle: Work in your group. Be ready to say why.
slides.time_note: SoW Part C is 10 minutes (8 to sort, then justify and photograph). Trimmed to 8 in all.

items: Has a nucleus
DNA floats freely
Has mitochondria
Found in bacteria
Has no membrane-bound nucleus
Has ribosomes
DNA is inside a nucleus
Has an endoplasmic reticulum
Found in animal cells
Found in plant cells
Has no membrane-bound organelles
Has membrane-bound organelles

blocks.text: Sort into two columns: PROKARYOTE and EUKARYOTE.
items: Photograph or sketch your sorted table.

do: Give each group a set of 12 feature cards. Copy the 12 cards from the slide onto paper strips if you do not have printed sets.
Groups of 3 or 4 sort the cards into two columns on their desk.
After the timer, cold-call one group for each disputed card. Then ask groups to photograph or sketch their sorted table.
Note any card that is wrong in most groups. Use this in the first Explain slide.
say: Sort these into Prokaryote or Eukaryote. Be ready to justify every card.
Group by the door, where did you put 'Has no membrane-bound nucleus', and why?
look_for: Note any card that most groups place wrongly. For example, 'Has ribosomes' placed only under Eukaryote.
Check 2 or 3 groups: each can give a reason for every card.
if_then: If a group is stuck, say: Look at the three diagrams. Is this part in the bacterium? Is it in the animal or plant cell?
If a card is true for both, say: Hold that thought. Be ready to say why it is a hard card.
If a group puts a card in the wrong column, do not correct. Say: Be ready to justify it. We will check it together.
notes.why_this_works: Moving cards makes thinking visible and shows where groups disagree. Arguing about a card is where much of the learning happens. Misconception addressed: all cells have a nucleus.
answer_key: Prokaryote: DNA floats freely; Found in bacteria; Has no membrane-bound nucleus; Has no membrane-bound organelles.
Eukaryote: Has a nucleus; Has mitochondria; DNA is inside a nucleus; Has an endoplasmic reticulum; Found in animal cells; Found in plant cells; Has membrane-bound organelles.
Both: Has ribosomes (a hard card; learners may place it between the two columns).

slides.title: What the card sort showed
slides.subtitle: Look at the diagrams with me.
slides.time_note: Start of the SoW direct instruction (12 minutes in all, trimmed to 9).

blocks.text: Where did your group put 'Has ribosomes'? Look at the bacterium. Is it there too?

items: Prokaryote :: No membrane-bound nucleus. DNA floats freely.
Eukaryote :: DNA inside a nucleus. Membrane-bound organelles.
Both :: Cell membrane. Ribosomes.

do: Show the bacterium diagram again (previous slides) while you speak, then return to this slide.
Reveal the three columns one click at a time.
Use the cards that most groups got wrong in the sort. Ribosomes is the example in the SoW.
The ARES video (observe.video) may be played here, after the card sort, if time allows. Preview it first. Do not play it before the card sort.
say: Let me address what I saw during the card sort. Ribosomes: almost every group put these under Eukaryote only. Let's look at the diagram together.
Ribosomes are actually present in both. This matters. It means even the simplest bacteria can make proteins.
That's why bacteria in an infected wound can be so dangerous. They are making proteins too.
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds after the question, before you show the answer.
look_for: Learners who got ribosomes wrong now change their cards. Ask a group that placed it correctly to say why.
if_then: If learners say 'bacteria are too simple to have ribosomes', say: Look at the bacterium diagram. Point to the ribosomes. What do ribosomes help the cell make?
notes.why_this_works: Using learners' own sorting errors makes the teaching match what they need. They see the correct idea against the cards they placed themselves.
notes.science_note: The slide names three key differences from the SoW: nuclear membrane, organelles and how DNA is organised.

slides.title: Cell theory: three ideas
slides.subtitle: Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow each added a piece.
slides.time_note: Middle part of the SoW direct instruction.

items: microscope :: All living things are made of cells.
puzzle :: The cell is the basic unit of life.
arrows_cycle :: All cells arise from pre-existing cells.

blocks.text: Schleiden: plants. Schwann: animals. Virchow: all cells from cells.

do: Write the three tenets word for word on the board.
Reveal them one click at a time. After each one, link to the table learners filled in.
say: Matthias Schleiden was a botanist. He studied plant cells.
Theodor Schwann studied animal cells.
Rudolf Virchow said: Omnis cellula e cellula. All cells come from cells.
Many people built this idea over time. No one person did it alone.
look_for: Learners copy the tenets correctly into notebooks.
if_then: If learners mix up the scientists, say: Check your Evidence Table. Which one said all cells come from cells?
notes.why_this_works: Naming the theory after learners have worked with the evidence helps them see what the words describe. Misconception addressed: scientific ideas come from one person.

slides.title: Colour-code your diagrams
slides.subtitle: Use the three colours.
slides.time_note: End of the SoW direct instruction (12 minutes in all, trimmed to 9).

items: GREEN :: Present in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes
BLUE :: Eukaryotes only
RED :: Plant eukaryotes only

do: Learners use their ARES diagram cards or printed sheets. They can also look back at the diagram slides.
Learners colour or underline each label GREEN, BLUE or RED.
Check ribosomes and cell wall first.
say: Now colour-code your diagrams. Green is in both. Blue is eukaryotes only. Red is plant eukaryotes only.
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds after each prompt before you help.
look_for: Check 8 to 10 diagrams: ribosomes are GREEN (not BLUE) and the cell wall is RED. Address any other answer with that learner.
if_then: If ribosomes are BLUE, say: Look at the bacterium. Are ribosomes there? What colour should they be?
If a learner asks about the cell wall in the bacterium, say: Good eye. Write your question on a yellow note for the Driving Question Board.
notes.why_this_works: Colour coding turns a diagram into a sorting task, which makes patterns easy to see and remember.
answer_key: GREEN: cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes.
BLUE: nucleus, mitochondrion, endoplasmic reticulum.
RED: cell wall, vacuole.

slides.title: Back to our predictions
slides.subtitle: Mark your ideas in a different colour.
slides.time_note: Added from the manual: return to predictions. Not a separate SoW activity.

items: pencil :: Read your 'I think all cells share…' sentences.
check :: Mark ideas that fit today's evidence.
cross :: Mark ideas that do not fit.

do: Point to the BEFORE — Our Predictions column and the hands-up count you wrote.
Learners use a different colour pen to mark each idea.
Ask for the same hands-up count again.
say: Look back at what you wrote. Use a different colour. Mark each idea right or wrong, using what you saw today.
Hands up: who wrote that every cell has a nucleus? Does that fit today's evidence?
look_for: Learners mark at least one idea as right or wrong. Check 6 notebooks.
if_then: If a learner marks every idea 'right', say: Check the card sort. Does your idea fit the bacterium?
notes.why_this_works: Marking their own earlier ideas shows learners that their thinking has changed. Misconception addressed: all cells have a nucleus.
answer_key: Example: Membrane: right (all cells have one). DNA: right (both cell types have it). Nucleus in every cell: wrong (bacteria have no membrane-bound nucleus).

slides.title: Explain how Amina's body made new skin cells
slides.subtitle: Write four sentences: Claim, Evidence, Reasoning.
slides.time_note: SoW: 8 minutes of silent writing. Trimmed to 6.

blocks.text: Use cell theory to explain how Amina's body made new skin cells to close the wound.

items: Claim :: How did Amina's body make new skin cells?
Evidence :: Name a scientist or an idea from cell theory.
Reasoning :: Explain why. Use 'because' or 'therefore'.

do: Learners write alone in their notebooks.
Start the 6:00 timer.
Circulate and read. At the end, collect 6 notebooks (two from each ability group) for rapid review.
say: Using your colour-coded diagram, write a CER paragraph.
Your Claim answers: How did Amina's body make new skin cells?
Your Evidence comes from Virchow's idea. Your Reasoning explains how.
notes.wait_time: The full 6 minutes of silent writing.
look_for: Each paragraph has a clear Claim sentence, evidence naming a scientist or tenet, and Reasoning with 'therefore' or 'because' that links to Amina's healing.
Collect 6 notebooks (two from each ability group) and check them quickly.
if_then: If a learner is stuck, say: What did Virchow say about where new cells come from? Start there.
If the writing is general, say: Which cells are we talking about? Which cells made the new skin cells?
notes.why_this_works: CER moves learners from 'Virchow said…' to 'so Amina's body could…'. It makes them use the idea to explain the phenomenon. Misconception addressed: new cells appear from nothing.
answer_key: Amina's body made new skin cells from skin cells that were already there. Virchow's cell theory says all cells arise from pre-existing cells. The living skin cells next to the cut divided to make new cells. Therefore the wound closed because new skin cells came from existing skin cells.
notes.science_note: You do not need to name cell division processes yet. It is enough that learners say cells divide to make new cells.

slides.title: Share your reasoning
slides.subtitle: Listen. Show a thumb.
slides.time_note: SoW: cold-call 2 learners and a thumbs check (trimmed to 1 minute).

blocks.text: Does the Reasoning clearly connect cell theory to Amina's healing?

items: thinking :: Listen for the Claim, the Evidence and the Reasoning.
raised_hand :: Thumbs up if the Reasoning clearly links to Amina.

do: Cold-call 2 learners to read their CER aloud. Pick one with a strong, clear answer and one whose Reasoning is still short, so the class can compare.
Ask them to read only the Reasoning sentence if time is short.
After each reading, ask for thumbs.
say: Please read your CER aloud.
Thumbs up if their Reasoning clearly connects cell theory to the phenomenon.
look_for: Count the thumbs. Do most learners agree the Reasoning links cell theory to Amina?
Check if learners can say why the Reasoning works or not.
if_then: If few thumbs go up, say: What is missing? What could they add to link Virchow to Amina's finger?
notes.why_this_works: Hearing a classmate's reasoning shows learners what a good explanation sounds like. Judging it makes them think about the connection themselves.

slides.title: Driving Question Board
slides.subtitle: Add a note. Add a star.
slides.time_note: SoW: 4 minutes of silent reflection.

blocks.text: Why do cells in our body look so different from each other — and how does the shape of a cell determine the job it can do?

items: question :: Yellow note: a NEW question from today
lightbulb :: Green note: something you saw today that helps
star :: Star: a Lesson 1 question we have started to answer

do: Read the driving question aloud with the class.
Hand out sticky notes in two colours: yellow for new questions, green for growing understanding.
Learners go to the board in turns to post and add stars.
After the timer, photograph the board for planning.
say: We've been learning about cell theory and cell structure today. Look at our Driving Question Board. Has today's lesson answered any of the questions from Lesson 1? If so, put a star on it.
Then write your own note. Either a new question or a sentence that shows your thinking has grown. Use something you saw today.
notes.wait_time: The full 4 minutes of silent writing.
look_for: Every learner posts at least one note. A missing note means possible disengagement or confusion. Follow up.
Check the green notes for accuracy. A note such as 'all cells are the same' is a misconception. Correct it before Lesson 3.
if_then: If a learner writes 'all cells are the same', say: Look at your sorted cards. Are prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells exactly the same? Rewrite your note.
If a learner has no idea what to write, say: What surprised you today? Start with that.
notes.why_this_works: A public board makes thinking visible and shows the class that science keeps asking questions. The two colours show the teacher the balance between confusion and understanding.
answer_key: Yellow note example: If all cells come from pre-existing cells, where did the first cell come from?
Green note example: I saw that both the bacterium and the animal cell have a cell membrane and ribosomes, so all cells share some basic parts.

slides.title: Does our evidence answer it yet?
slides.subtitle: Listen to some notes. Then vote.
slides.time_note: Reading aloud 3 to 4 notes (SoW) plus a quick vote (manual).

blocks.text: A classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes with small gold stars beside some of them.
items: dqb_sticky_notes_board
A friendly flat cartoon of a classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes, with three small gold stars stuck beside some notes, and a wooden desk with a pot of pencils in front.

blocks.text: Hands up: Yes, or Not yet?

do: Read 3 or 4 notes aloud quickly. Include at least one question note.
Point to the driving question.
Ask for a hands-up vote: Does the evidence we have today answer the driving question yet? Count Yes and Not yet.
say: Listen to this question from the back table: If all cells come from pre-existing cells, where did the FIRST cell come from? That is a brilliant scientific question that researchers still debate.
Does the evidence on our board answer the big question yet? Yes, or not yet?
We still haven't answered the big one. Hold it. We'll get there.
look_for: Most learners vote 'Not yet'. Ask one or two why. Look for the idea that all cells share parts but we still have not explained why they look different.
if_then: If many vote 'Yes', say: What evidence do we have for why a blood cell looks different from a skin cell? What is still missing?
notes.why_this_works: Voting on whether evidence is enough teaches learners to judge claims by evidence. It shows them the board is a working record, not a finished answer.

slides.title: Your cell model: Version 1
slides.subtitle: Scientists use models. Models are never perfect.
slides.time_note: Quick introduction to the SoW model task (about 12 minutes in all across the next two slides).

items: memo :: Heading: VERSION 1 and the date
pencil :: Sketch and label 8 parts
book :: Model Key: one sentence for each label
thinking :: Limitation Statement: 2 gaps

do: Display the Version 1 checklist (this slide) on the board: 8 required labels, 1 sentence per label in the Key, 1 Limitation Statement with at least 2 gaps.
Explain that each learner keeps ONE model for the whole unit and revises it in a new colour each lesson.
say: Every scientist who studies cells uses models. Models are never perfect, but they capture what we know right now.
Today you will draw Version 1 of YOUR cell model. By Lesson 12, this same page will be full of revisions, additions and corrections. That's what science looks like.
look_for: Learners know the four things to do before they start.
if_then: If learners ask whether to draw a plant or an animal cell, say: Choose one. Label the parts your cell has.
notes.why_this_works: Showing the checklist first makes the task clear. Telling learners the model will change builds expectation and shows them that models are for revising.

slides.title: Draw Version 1 of your cell model
slides.subtitle: Work silently. Use a pen, because you will add a new colour later.
slides.time_note: SoW: 12 minutes for the whole model task. 9 here for the sketch and Key; the limits and partner share follow on the next slide.

blocks.text: Sketch and label a generalised eukaryotic cell. You may choose plant or animal.
items: Labels: cell membrane · cell wall (if plant) · nucleus · cytoplasm · mitochondria · ribosomes · vacuole (if plant) · endoplasmic reticulum
pencil :: Draw the cell on a full page.
memo :: Write the Model Key under your sketch.
book :: One sentence for each label: its role.

do: Learners use a full blank page in their science notebook.
Tell them: This is your scientific record. Work silently and independently.

Circulate with the checklist. Narrate what you see: I see a learner has labelled the mitochondria and written that it produces energy. I see another learner has drawn a cell wall on an animal cell. Let's check that.
Collect all models at the end of the lesson, photograph them for records and return them next lesson.
say: You have about 12 minutes for the whole model task: the sketch, the Key and your limits. Start with the sketch and the Key. Work silently and independently. This is YOUR scientific record.
Count your labels. How many do you have?
Check: do animal cells have cell walls?
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds after a correction prompt, so the learner can self-correct.
look_for: Check 8 to 10 notebooks with the checklist: all 8 required labels are present (cell wall and vacuole only for plant cells).
Each Model Key sentence says the structure AND its function. 'Nucleus: oval shape, contains DNA, controls cell activities' is adequate. 'Nucleus: it's in the middle' is not enough.
Animal cells are not drawn with a cell wall. The nucleus is drawn as a clear structure.
if_then: If labels are missing, say: Count your labels. How many do you have? Which ones are missing?
If a Key sentence says only where the part is, say: Where it is tells me nothing about what it does. What is its job?
If an animal cell has a cell wall, say: Check the animal cell diagram. Do animal cells have cell walls?
notes.why_this_works: A dated, revisable model gives learners a record they can improve all unit. Writing a Key sentence forces them to link structure to function. Misconception addressed: animal cells have cell walls.
answer_key: Sketch with labels: cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum (plus cell wall and vacuole if plant).
Cell membrane: thin boundary that controls what enters and leaves the cell.
Cell wall (plant): strong outer layer that supports the cell.
Nucleus: oval shape, contains DNA, controls cell activities.
Cytoplasm: jelly-like part where many reactions happen.
Mitochondria: release energy from food for the cell to use.
Ribosomes: make proteins.
Vacuole (plant): stores water and dissolved substances.
Endoplasmic reticulum: network that moves materials around the cell.

slides.title: The limits of my model
slides.subtitle: Scientists say what they do not know yet.
slides.time_note: SoW: Limitation Statement and a 2-minute partner share, plus a next-lesson prediction added from the manual.

blocks.text: At the bottom of your page write: This model does not yet show…
items: List at least 2 gaps.
Share with your partner. Add one of their gaps.
Last, write: Next lesson, I predict… because…

do: Learners write their Limitation Statement, then share with a partner.
Ask them to add one of their partner's gaps if they had not thought of it.
Ask for one sentence predicting the next lesson. Then collect all Version 1 models.
say: Read your partner's limitation. Do you agree those are real gaps? Add one of their gaps to your own list if you hadn't thought of it.
Last, write one sentence: Next lesson, I predict… because…
notes.wait_time: 20 seconds of silent writing before the partner share.
look_for: Check 8 to 10 notebooks: at least 2 honest gaps are listed. Accept any scientifically honest statement.
Each learner has one sentence predicting the next lesson.
if_then: If a learner cannot think of a gap, say: What do you still not know about how the cell membrane or the nucleus works? Write that.
If the prediction has no reason, say: Add a 'because'. What did you see today that makes you think that?
notes.why_this_works: Saying what a model cannot yet explain keeps learners from thinking they are finished. It also gives them a reason to look forward to the next lesson.
answer_key: This model does not yet show how the cell membrane decides what to let in. It does not yet show how the nucleus talks to the rest of the cell.
Next lesson, I predict we will compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells in more detail, because today was only the start.

lesson_oneliner: Find out what all cells share, and learn the three big ideas of cell theory.
purpose: Learners meet the cell as the basic unit of life. They learn the three ideas of cell theory from Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow.
They compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells using labelled diagrams and a card sort.
They use the ugali kitchen picture to make new cell words easier to remember.
They connect cell theory to the healing cut: new skin cells come from skin cells that were already there.
They draw Version 1 of their cell model. They keep this one page and revise it in a new colour in every lesson.
before_class: Display the phenomenon image of Amina's healing finger on the board before learners enter.
Prepare 12 feature cards per group (copy them from the card sort slide onto paper strips if there are no printed sets). The SoW gives no group numbers.
Prepare printed A3 diagram sheets or ARES resource cards: animal cell, plant cell, prokaryotic cell. Include a short reading on the three scientists with countries and periods.
Have sticky notes in two colours (yellow and green) and star stickers ready for the Driving Question Board.
Write the Version 1 checklist where all learners can see it (8 labels, 1 Key sentence per label, 1 Limitation Statement with 2 gaps).
Have green, blue and red pencils ready for colour-coding. Learners need a pen for the model and a different colour for marking predictions.
Preview observe.video (Khan Academy, Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells) before class. Do not play it until after the card sort.
Decide where to photograph the Driving Question Board and the Version 1 models at the end.
do_not_show: Do not play the ARES video observe.video (Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells) until after learners finish the card sort. It can give away the sort answers.
Do not show the slides 'What the card sort showed' or 'Colour-code your diagrams' until after learners have sorted their cards.
Do not give learners the ARES readings on prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells (predict.reading, observe.reading) before the card sort.
Do not show or read out the answer key (countries, dates, colour key, model answers) while learners are still writing.
so_far: In Lesson 1 we met Amina's healing finger and asked why cells look so different.
goals: State the three ideas of cell theory and the scientists who built them.
Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells using their structures.
Describe a cell by sketching and labelling Version 1 of your cell model.

key_words.definition: The basic unit of life. All living things are made of cells.
Three big ideas about cells, built by many scientists over time.
Comparing something new to something you already know.
A drawing or idea that shows how something works. We can improve it.

resource_notes.note: This video gives away the prokaryote and eukaryote differences students should find themselves. Use after the card sort, at 'What the card sort showed'.
The reading explains prokaryote and eukaryote features, which would pre-empt the prediction. Use after 'What the card sort showed' as consolidation reading.
Practice questions on prokaryotes and eukaryotes need the content first. Use after 'Colour-code your diagrams' to check understanding.
On topic for Explain but goes deep into organelle functions. Check it does not go beyond Version 1 labels; organelles are Lessons 4 and 5.
Khan Academy practice on prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells fits Explain consolidation after the card sort. Quick check that its level suits Grade 10.
Plant versus animal comparison is mostly Lesson 5 content. Use it in Lesson 5 when learners compare plant and animal cells.
Introductory cell practice may help learners judge what the evidence answers. Preview to check it matches 'Does our evidence answer it yet?' and avoids new content.
Endosymbiosis theory is beyond Grade 10 and Version 1 needs, and no lesson in this unit teaches it.
Cell theory practice supports Version 1 model-building by securing the three tenets. Check the questions stay at Grade 10 level.

summary.observe_prompt: Name the diagrams you studied and what you did with the cards.
summary.learn_prompt: Write the three ideas of cell theory and one difference between the two kinds of cell.
summary.explain_prompt: How does Virchow's idea explain the new skin cells on Amina's finger?
summary.next_lesson: We compare a bacterium and a human cell more closely.
summary.answer_observe: I studied labelled diagrams of an animal cell, a plant cell and a prokaryotic cell such as E. coli. I sorted feature cards into Prokaryote and Eukaryote. I matched parts of the ugali kitchen to parts of the cell.
summary.answer_learn: Cell theory has three ideas: all living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow each added to it. Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Prokaryotic cells do not.
summary.answer_explain: Amina's body made new skin cells because of Virchow's idea that all cells come from pre-existing cells. The living skin cells next to the cut made new skin cells. Therefore the wound closed. My Version 1 cell model shows the main cell parts and what each does. It also lists what the model does not yet show.
reflection: During the card sort, which cards did most groups place wrongly? Does your Lesson 3 plan deal with them?
In the CER paragraphs you collected, did learners connect Virchow's idea to new skin cells, or write about cells in general? If general, plan a 5-minute revisit at the start of Lesson 3.
How many yellow (question) and green (understanding) notes are on the board? If yellow heavily outnumbers green, plan a consolidation activity.
In the Version 1 models, did any learners draw a cell wall on an animal cell? Is the nucleus drawn as a clear structure?
Did you hold the full wait time, or did you answer for learners?

do: Use this slide at the end of the lesson or set it as homework. Allow at most 2 minutes in class.
Learners write one or two sentences under each heading in their notebooks.
Ask for one or two volunteers to read an answer aloud.
say: Answer the three questions in your notebook. What did you observe? What did you learn? How does this explain Amina's healing finger?
Use words from today: cell theory, prokaryotic and eukaryotic.
notes.why_this_works: Writing the three answers in the learner's own words shows what they understood. The last question links the lesson back to the healing cut.

do: Point to Lesson 2 on the map and to the YOU ARE HERE marker.
Read the So far line aloud.
Read the unit driving question aloud. Keep this to about 1 minute.
say: Last lesson we met Amina's healing finger and asked why cells look so different.
Today we find out what all cells have in common. That is the first step towards the big question.
Look at the driving question. We cannot answer it yet. Today we build the base.
unit_map_notes.why_this_works: Showing where today fits helps learners see the lesson as part of one story. Repeating the driving question keeps the healing cut in mind.

do: Read the three goals aloud with the class.
Read each key word and its meaning once. Do not teach them in depth now.
Keep this to about 1 minute.
say: By the end of today you can state the three ideas of cell theory, compare two kinds of cell and draw Version 1 of your cell model.
These four words will come up today: cell, cell theory, analogy and model. You will use them as we go.
goals_notes.why_this_works: Short goals tell learners what success looks like. The key words are only the ones needed to understand the task. You teach the other words when learners meet them on a slide.
